'''Melvin Isaac Simon''' (born February 8, 1937, in New York City) is an American molecular biologist, molecular geneticist, and [[microbiologist]].

==Biography==
After secondary education at Manhattan's [[Yeshiva University High School for Boys]],<ref name=interview>{{cite web|url=https://collections.archives.caltech.edu/repositories/2/digital_objects/61|title=Simon, Melvin I. Interview by Shirley K. Cohen. Pasadena, California, May 24 and June 5, 2005. Oral History Project|website=California Institute of Technology Archives}}</ref> he graduated in 1959 with a B.S. from [[City College of New York]] and in 1963 with a Ph.D. from [[Brandeis University]]. From 1963 to 1965 he was a postdoc at [[Princeton University]]. From 1965 to 1982 he was a faculty member of the biology department of the [[University of California, San Diego]] (UCSD).<ref name=AmericanAcademy>{{cite web|title=Biography. Melvin I. Simon|website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|date=6 December 2023 |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/melvin-i-simon}}</ref> In 1982 he and UCSD professor [[John Abelson|John Abelson founded the Agouron Institute]]. In 1982 Simon and Abelson both moved to [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech). In the Division of Biology of Caltech, Simon was Biaggini Professor of Biological Sciences from 1982 to 2013, when he retired from Caltech as professor emeritus. At Caltech he was the chair of his department from 1995 to 2000. At the [[UC San Diego School of Medicine]], was an adjunct professor of pharmacology from 2013 when he retired from UCSD.<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/melvin-i-simon-xi5rk4/|title=Melvin I. Simon |website=Member Directory, National Academy of Sciences}}</ref>

Simon is the author or coauthor of over 350 scientific publications.<ref name=AmericanAcademy/> Simon's group at UCSD did important research on bacterial movement and [[chemotaxis]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/0300-9084(89)90105-3|title=Protein phosphorylation in the bacterial chemotaxis system |year=1989 |last1=Simon |first1=Melvin I. |last2=Borkovich |first2=Katherine A. |last3=Bourret |first3=Robert B. |last4=Hess |first4=J.Fred |journal=Biochimie |volume=71 |issue=9–10 |pages=1013–1019 |pmid=2512992 }}</ref><ref name=AmericanAcademy/> Michael Robert Silverman (born in 1943)<ref>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |author=Silverman, Michael Robert|title=Characterization and genetic analysis of flagellar mutants in Escherichia coli|year= 1972 |publisher=University of California, San Diego |url=https://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=US201300325178 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221125132414/https://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=US201300325178 |archive-date=2022-11-25}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Michael R. Silverman and Bonnie L. Bassler Win 2011 Paul Ehrlich and Ludwig Darmstaedter Prize|date=28 January 2011|website=Goethe Universität, Frankfurt am Main|url=https://aktuelles.uni-frankfurt.de/englisch/michael-r-silverman-and-bonnie-l-bassler-win-2021-paul-ehrlich-and-ludwig-darmstaedter-prize/}}</ref> and Melvin Simon are credited with the discovery that bacterial flagella are based in [[rotating locomotion in living systems|rotary motor]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Silverman M, Simon M | title = Flagellar rotation and the mechanism of bacterial motility | journal = Nature | volume = 249 | issue = 452 | pages = 73–4 | date = May 1974 | pmid = 4598030 | doi = 10.1038/249073a0 | bibcode = 1974Natur.249...73S | s2cid = 10370084 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1146/annurev.mi.31.100177.002145|title=Bacterial Flagella |year=1977 |last1=Silverman |first1=M. |last2=Simon |first2=M. I. |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |volume=31 |pages=397–419 |pmid=410356 }}</ref><ref name=AmericanAcademy/> Silverman was Simon's doctoral student.<ref>{{cite web|title=Melvin I. Simon, Ph.D.|website=Chemistry Tree|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=34929}}</ref>

Simon's laboratory group at Caltech played an important role in the [[Human Genome Project]] (HGP) and built many of the initial [[Library (biology)|libraries]] that provided the basic material for the HGP.<ref name=AmericanAcademy/> Simon's group invented in 1992 [[bacterial artificial chromosome]]s (BACs) and in 1994 phage artificial chromosomes (PACs) using the [[P1 phage]].<ref>{{cite book|author=McElheny, Victor K.|author-link=Victor K. McElheny|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6z-mNS3H2w8C&q=simon+lab+also+invented+artificial+chromosomes| isbn=978-0-465-03260-0 | title=Drawing the Map of Life: Inside the Human Genome Project | date=31 July 2012 | publisher=Basic Books |page=106}}</ref> The group's scientists were among the main developers of the maps of [[human chromosome 16]] and [[human chromosome 22]].<ref name=AmericanAcademy/> In 2002 Simon and colleagues determined the complete genome sequence of ''[[Pyrobaculum aerophilum]]'', a [[hyperthermophilic]] [[archaeum]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1073/pnas.241636498|title=Genome sequence of the hyperthermophilic crenarchaeon ''Pyrobaculum aerophilum'' |year=2002 |last1=Fitz-Gibbon |first1=Sorel T. |last2=Ladner |first2=Heidi |last3=Kim |first3=Ung-Jin |last4=Stetter |first4=Karl O. |last5=Simon |first5=Melvin I. |last6=Miller |first6=Jeffrey H. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=99 |issue=2 |pages=984–989 |pmid=11792869 |pmc=117417 |bibcode=2002PNAS...99..984F |doi-access=free }}</ref> Simon and his Caltech group gained an international reputation for their research on [[G-protein]]s and the molecular mechanisms of how these proteins are essential for transmitting signals detected on cellular surfaces into cellular interiors.<ref name=AmericanAcademy/><ref name=NAS/> Simon and colleagues demonstrated how various genetic mutations in bacteria, [[nematode]]s, and mice cause various abnormalities and diseases.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbe.caltech.edu/people/melvin-i-mel-simon|title=Melvin I. (Mel) Simon|website=Division of Biology and Biological Engineering, Caltech}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/S0896-6273(00)80123-3|title=Mutations in a ''C. elegans'' G<sub>q</sub>α Gene Disrupt of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=106 |issue=27 |pages=11330–11335 |pmid=19564617 |pmc=2708751 |bibcode=2009PNAS..10611330I |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Simon has been involved with a number of non-profit organizations and commercial corporations. He was one of the founders of [[Agouron Pharmaceuticals]], Inc.,<ref name=AmericanAcademy/> which was acquired by [[Warner-Lambert]] in 1999.<ref>{{cite news|author=Jacobs, Paul|date=January 27, 1999|title=Biotech Firm Agouron Will be Purchased for $2.1 Billion|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-jan-27-fi-2112-story.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Morrow, David J.|author-link=David J. Morrow|title=Warner-Lambert to Acquire Agouron Pharmaceuticals|date=January 27, 1999|newspaper=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/01/27/business/warner-lambert-to-acquire-agouron-pharmaceuticals.html}}</ref> He was also one of the founders of the Diversa Corporation,<ref name=AmericanAcademy/> which was merged with the Celunol Corporation in 2007 to form the [[Verenium Corporation]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Diversa and Celunol Complete Merger to Create Verenium Corporation|date=June 20, 2007|website=Biospace|url=https://www.biospace.com/b-diversa-b-and-b-celunol-b-complete-merger-to-create-verenium-corporation}}</ref> He was one of the founders for Agouron Institute and served as President from its founding in 1978 and became Chairman of the Board from 1987 through 2024. He was a co-editor of Methods in Enzymology from 1987 to 2010. 

Simon was a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim fellow]] for the academic year 1978–1979.<ref>{{cite web|title=Melvin I. Simon|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/melvin-i-simon/}}</ref> He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1985<ref name=NAS/> and a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1986.<ref name=AmericanAcademy/> In 1991 he received the [[Selman A. Waksman Award in Microbiology]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Selman A. Waksman Award in Microbiology|website=National Academy of Sciences|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/waksman-award-in-microbiology.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111126045248/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/waksman-award-in-microbiology.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 26, 2011}}</ref>

In June 1959 in the Bronx, he married Linda Fried. They have two sons and a daughter.
